situation:
You are a high-school senior working weekends at a grocery store, and your first paychecks land in a mobile payment account on your phone, where the balance earns nothing at all. This afternoon you are meeting a teller (judge) at BLUE HERON SAVINGS BANK, which has offered you your first credit card.

You take home about $520 a month. Last fall your older sister lent you $700 for a laptop you needed for coursework. She is saving to move into her own apartment in the spring and has asked when the money will come back to her. You have set nothing aside for yourself since you started the job.

One course is to repay your sister $175 a month out of your pay and clear the $700 in four months. That owes no interest to anyone, but it leaves you nothing set aside, so a car repair before graduation would go onto the new credit card at its high rate.

The other course is to accept the card, hand your sister the full $700 now, and repay the card at $65 a month for twelve months, which adds roughly $80 in interest. The smaller monthly payment frees $100 a month for a savings account that pays interest. The teller (judge) wants your recommendation.

The teller (judge) will greet you and ask to hear your ideas. After you have presented and answered the teller's questions, the teller (judge) will thank you for your work.
judgeCharacterization:
You are a teller at BLUE HERON SAVINGS BANK. Business background is the same as the situation above.

A high-school senior with a first part-time paycheck, an offer of a first credit card, and $700 owed to an older sister is deciding between clearing that debt quickly and starting to save. You want to hear how the money now sitting in a mobile payment account should be handled, who else the decision touches, and a clear recommendation.

After the participant has presented, you are to ask the following questions of each participant:
judgeQuestions: Six months from now, what would be different for your sister?
If a lot more people start borrowing money, what happens to the rate a bank pays on your savings?
